Are liberation theology, feminism compatible?
-- 2/27/97

Ecumenical News International

LIMA, Peru -- The differing views of two highly prominent theologians -- one from North America, the other 
from Latin America -- have raised the issue of the compatibility of feminist theology and liberation theology.

The issue was raised after a visit October 1996 by one of the founders of feminist theology, Rosemary 
Radford Ruether, a Roman Catholic professor at Garrett-Evangelical Theological Seminary in Evanston, Ill., to Lima 
where she met leaders of the Women's Ecumenical Round Table and the Catholic Talitha Cumi Movement. 

Differences discovered

After her visit, Dr. Ruether wrote in the 
National Catholic 
Reporter
 that one of the unfortunate facts that she 
had discovered in Lima was the difference made by fellow theologian the Rev. Gustavo Gutierrez between 
liberation theology and feminist movements. Dr. Gutierrez, a Peruvian Catholic priest, is generally seen as the father of 
liberation theology.

According to Dr. Ruether, Dr. Gutierrez insists that feminism is foreign to Latin American thinking and 
distracts people from the fundamental concern for the poor. She added that Dr. Gutierrez and staff at a leading Catholic 
institute in Lima had essentially not worked with local Protestants, despite Protestant support for liberation theology. 

According to the Latin American and Caribbean Communication Agency, Dr. Ruether further said that Dr. 
Gutierrez had not considered spirituality from the perspective of indigenous people. It was most surprising, she said, that 
Dr. Gutierrez continued to speak of indigenous people from the Spanish Catholic perspective, ignoring the fact 
that Peru's indigenous peoples had found their own voice.

Deserved praise

Dr. Ruether claimed that Dr. Gutierrez's attitude was related to his interest in keeping liberation theology 
within institutional Catholicism rather than venturing out into new areas such as feminism, sexuality, reproduction, 
ecology, Protestant belief and indigenous religions. All these elements, she said, were out of favor with conservative Catholics.

The U.S. woman theologian acknowledged that Dr. Gutierrez deserved praise as the founder of a movement 
which reconnected theology with social justice. But she said it was sad to see him bowing to the "absolute" domination of 
a right-wing church.

Dr. Ruether said the future belonged to those who were integrating issues such as gender, ecology, ecumenism 
and indigenous spirituality.
